title: 5  Reproducible Research
text:
5.1 Why Reproducibility Matters
In this area you will learn how to: document your analysis, combine code, text and results in Quarto, organise and share your work using GitHub and make your analytical process transparent and reproducible. This chapter leans more heavily on external open resources than Chapters 1–4, because reproducibility is best learned by doing it in your own project, not by working through another isolated exercise dataset.
A result you cannot reproduce is a result no one — including future you — can fully trust. In environmental science specifically, claims often feed into policy; being able to show exactly how a number was produced, from raw download to final figure, is part of the scientific claim itself, not an optional extra.
The FAIR principles, widely used in Open Science, capture this as a checklist for data and code: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable. A well-organised Quarto + GitHub project addresses all four almost automatically.

title: 5  Reproducible Research
text: Analogy: a recipe that only works because the cook “just knows” to add a pinch of an unlisted ingredient is not a reproducible recipe, however good the dish tastes. A reproducible analysis is a recipe precise enough that someone else, in a different kitchen, gets the same dish.

title: 5  Reproducible Research
text:
5.2 From Scripts to Literate Programming
A plain .R script separates code from explanation — comments help, but the reasoning usually lives in your head or a separate document. Literate programming (the idea behind Quarto and R Markdown before it) interleaves narrative text, code and the code’s output — tables, figures, model summaries — in a single document that renders to HTML, PDF or a website. This entire module is one example; your final report and dashboard should be another.






Get started with Quarto



The official Quarto guide covers installation and the basics in under 30 minutes. If you already know R Markdown, the concepts transfer almost directly.



Guided task 5.2 — Your first Quarto document

Install Quarto (bundled with recent RStudio, or standalone from quarto.org).
Create a new .qmd file with a YAML header (title, author, format: html).
Add one text section, one code chunk that loads data/clean/dwd_climate_clean.csv and prints glimpse() and one ggplot2 figure.
Render it (quarto render your_file.qmd or the Render button in RStudio/Positron).

Reflect: what changed in how you wrote the analysis, compared to a plain script with separate comments?

title: 5  Reproducible Research
text:
5.3 Organising a Reproducible Project
Good project structure is a form of documentation in itself. A minimal, defensible layout:
my-challenge/
├── data/              # raw, locked data + a data dictionary (README.md)
├── R/                 # reusable functions, if any
├── analysis.qmd        # the literate-programming narrative (or several, numbered)
├── dashboard.qmd        # the interactive dashboard
├── _quarto.yml          # project configuration
└── README.md            # what this project is, how to run it
This directly extends the data-management principle from Chapter 1: the raw download never changes, every transformation is code and every code file has a clear place. Compare this module’s own repository structure — it follows exactly this pattern.

Ask your learning buddy to critique your folder structure against this checklist and to explain why a given convention exists (e.g. “why keep data/ separate from analysis code?”) rather than asking it to generate the structure for you sight unseen — you need to be able to justify your own project’s organisation in your report.

title: 5  Reproducible Research
section: 5.4 Version Control with Git and GitHub
text:
5.4 Version Control with Git and GitHub
Git tracks every change to your files over time; GitHub hosts that history online so others (and future you) can see it and so you have an off-machine backup. For this module, you need a working subset of Git, not the whole tool:

git init / cloning an existing repository
git add, git commit -m "message" — saving a snapshot with a clear description
git push / git pull — syncing with GitHub
Writing a short, useful README.md at the project root







Learn Git without the jargon



Happy Git and GitHub for the useR is written specifically for researchers coming from R and is the recommended path if this is your first time with version control. Work through its “Connect to GitHub” and first-commit chapters before your challenge deadline, not the night before.



Guided task 5.4 — Put your challenge under version control

Create a GitHub repository for your challenge analysis (public, CC-BY licence, unless your data source’s licence requires otherwise).
Commit your project in stages, with meaningful commit messages, as you go — not one giant commit at the end. Three to five commits across the challenge is a reasonable minimum.
Write a README.md that a stranger could use to understand what the project does and how to reproduce it, in under two minutes of reading.

Reflect: look at your own commit history. Would you, reading it back in six months, understand what each commit changed and why?



If the command line and git add/commit/push feel like too much at once before your deadline: GitHub Desktop gives you the same version control through a point-and-click interface — Happy Git and GitHub for the useR covers it alongside the command line.


If Git already feels comfortable and you want to understand why it works the way it does (branches, the object model, merging): Pro Git (free online) is the standard reference, far beyond what this module needs but useful for later projects.

title: 5  Reproducible Research
text:
5.5 Documentation and Open Science
Documentation is not an afterthought written at the end — it is the parts of §5.3’s project structure that explain themselves: a data dictionary next to the raw data (as in this module’s own data/README.md), comments explaining why a non-obvious cleaning decision was made (not just what the code does) and a README that states the project’s purpose, data sources and how to re-run it.
Open Science practice, concretely, for this module:

Publish your code and (where licensing allows) your data openly, with a clear licence (this module and its practice dataset are CC-BY 4.0).
Cite your data sources properly, including dataset codes and access dates (Eurostat datasets are versioned and updated — record when you pulled the data).
Make your dashboard and report’s methodology fully traceable back to the code that produced it — the requirement stated at the end of the overview.

title: 6  AI-Assisted Learning and Analysis
text:
6.1 AI as a Learning Navigator, Not an Answer Machine
In this area you will learn how to: work effectively with your AI learning buddy, formulate useful prompts, use AI to support coding and analysis, verify AI-generated suggestions and reflect critically on the role of AI in scientific work.
This module places AI at the centre of its “digital literacy” goal, not as a shortcut around learning but as practice for a skill you will use throughout your career: working productively with an AI system that does not simply hand you finished answers. Recall from the welcome page: your AI learning buddy structures problems, identifies competencies, recommends exercises, answers comprehension questions and supports interpretation and reflection. It does not select your methods, check your code for you, evaluate your data quality, interpret your results, or draw your scientific conclusions. Those stay yours.

title: 6  AI-Assisted Learning and Analysis
text:
6.2 Socratic Dialogue and Computational Offloading
This module’s AI approach is built on two linked ideas:

Socratic dialogue. Rather than asking your AI learning buddy “what’s the answer?”, you engage it in a back-and-forth: you propose an approach, it asks a clarifying or challenging question, you refine your thinking and so on. This mirrors how a good human tutor works: the value is in the questions, not just the final statement.
Computational offloading. You can legitimately hand off mechanical work to AI — boilerplate code, syntax lookups, first-draft phrasing — so you can spend your own cognitive effort on the parts that require judgement: which method fits the question, whether a result makes scientific sense, what a finding actually means.


Analogy: a calculator offloads arithmetic so you can focus on which calculation to run. AI can offload writing a ggplot2 boilerplate or a dplyr pipeline skeleton, so you can focus on which plot answers your research question and whether the numbers it produces make physical sense.

The distinction matters because the two are easy to blur: offloading the typing of a regression call is fine; offloading the decision of which predictors belong in your model, or what your R² means for your specific climate-data question, defeats the purpose of the module.

title: 6  AI-Assisted Learning and Analysis
text:
6.3 Prompt Literacy
A vague prompt gets a vague, generic answer. Prompt literacy is the skill of asking in a way that gets you a useful, checkable response — for coding and for conceptual questions alike.







Weak prompt
Stronger prompt




“Fix my code”
“This ggplot2 call throws object 'Sunshine_hours' not found. Here is my code and str(climate) output — what’s the mismatch?”


“Explain regression”
“I have a multiple regression with Sunshine_hours, Year and Region predicting Temperature_C. Explain what the Region coefficients mean, using my variable names.”


“Is my p-value good?”
“My hypothesis test gives p < 0.001 comparing temperature in 1991–2000 vs. 2015–2024 at n = 50 observations per group. Walk me through, step by step, what conclusions I can and cannot draw — including effect size.”



Notice the pattern: the stronger prompts give context (your actual variables, your actual numbers, your actual error message) and ask for reasoning, not just a verdict.

If you paste a lesson’s R code into your learning buddy and it “fixes” a line you didn’t ask about, don’t just accept the change — ask it to explain why the original line was wrong. If its explanation doesn’t hold up against what you learned in the chapter, the original line was probably fine.


Exercise 6.3 — Rewrite three weak prompts
Take three prompts you have actually typed into an AI tool during this module (or would be tempted to). For each, rewrite it following the pattern above: add concrete context and ask for the reasoning rather than only the answer.
Q1. Which of your three rewrites do you expect would produce the most different (and more useful) response from the original? Why?

title: 6  AI-Assisted Learning and Analysis
text:
6.4 Verifying AI-Generated Code and Explanations
AI-generated code and explanations can be wrong in ways that are easy to miss, because they are typically fluent and confident-sounding regardless of correctness. A working verification habit, for every substantial AI suggestion you use in this module:

Run it, don’t just read it. Does the code actually execute against your real data, or only against an imagined version of it?
Check the output against what you already know. Does a claimed “mean annual temperature of 45°C for Bayern” pass a basic sanity check against the ranges you saw in Chapter 2?
Ask “why”, not just “is this right”. A one-word confirmation from an AI tool is not verification. Ask it to explain why a line of code works and check that explanation against what you independently know.
Cross-check statistical claims against the module content. If an AI explanation of a p-value sounds like a yes/no verdict rather than the effect-size-plus-sample-size picture from Chapter 3, that’s a red flag, not a fact to copy into your report.


Exercise 6.4 — Spot the AI mistake
Below is a plausible-sounding but flawed AI explanation. Find the error(s) and correct them using what you’ve learned in this module.

“I ran lm(Temperature_C ~ Sunshine_hours, data = states) and got R² = 0.08 with p < 0.001, so sunshine duration clearly causes higher temperature in a strong, practically important way. Since p < 0.05, we can conclude the relationship is real and important.”

Q2. List every claim in this explanation that overreaches and explain — in your own words, referencing the relevant earlier chapter — what would need to be added or qualified for the statement to be defensible.

title: 7  Sustainability Problem Solving
text:
7.1 Why “Global” Matters: Data, Perspective and Responsibility
In this area you will learn how to: translate an environmental problem into an analytical question, use data as evidence, consider different possible explanations and develop an evidence-based response.
This chapter is different from Chapters 1–6: it is not primarily a set of techniques, but a way of thinking that connects them all back to why you’re doing this module in the first place — this module’s broader aim of environmental stewardship, taking responsibility for global challenges and actively contributing to solving them, not only analysing them from a distance.
Data never arrives from nowhere. Someone decided what to measure, who would measure it and which categories a value could fall into: decisions shaped by the priorities, language and institutions of wherever that data comes from. Working with a dataset from a context other than your own is a chance to notice your own frame of reference, the assumptions you bring to a number without realising you brought them (Mezirow, 1997). If a figure surprises you, or a category doesn’t map neatly onto what you expected, that moment of friction is worth sitting with rather than smoothing over. It is usually where real learning starts.
This module’s idea of environmental stewardship follows Global Citizenship Education’s emancipatory strand (Rieckmann, 2021): environmental problems and the data describing them are shared across borders rather than isolated to wherever they happen to be measured. A warming trend measured in one place and a shifting rainfall pattern measured somewhere else are two local readings of one connected global system. Practising that recognition is itself part of this competency area, alongside the technical skill of turning a broad problem into a data-answerable question.

title: 7  Sustainability Problem Solving
section: 7.2 From a Wicked Problem to an Analytical Question
text:
7.2 From a Wicked Problem to an Analytical Question
Real sustainability problems — shifting regional climates, urban heat stress, extreme weather becoming more frequent, biodiversity loss — start out broad, contested and not directly “answerable” with a dataset. The core move of this competency area is narrowing a broad problem into one specific, data-answerable question, without losing what made the problem matter in the first place.
Consider this example problem statement:

“Are the monitored weather stations showing signs of a shifting climate?”

This is not yet an analytical question — no single dataset or statistic settles it. A possible learning path, mirroring how your learning buddy would walk through it with you:

Your learning buddy asks: Which data would be relevant? Which variables do you need? How would you initially examine the data? → points you to Rubric 1, Understanding and Managing Data
Students work on: understanding variables, getting to know the dataset, checking data quality.
Your learning buddy, back at the problem: “Now that you understand the dataset, how could you explore possible patterns?” → Rubric 2, Exploring and Visualising Data
Your learning buddy: “Can you justify whether the 1991–2000-vs-2015–2024 difference you saw is meaningful, or could it just be random variation?” → Rubric 3, Statistical Inference
Your learning buddy: “Can you model the relationship between temperature and other climate variables and how much of the pattern each one explains?” → Rubric 4, Statistical Modelling
Your learning buddy, at the end: “Document your analysis and make it reproducible.” → Rubric 5, Reproducible Research

Notice what happened: the broad, contested problem (“is this safe?”) got narrowed into a sequence of specific, data-answerable sub-questions, each pointing to a competency area — without the original stewardship question disappearing. You return to it explicitly at the end (§7.4).

Exercise 7.1 — Narrow your own challenge
Take the Real-World Challenge you selected in the overview. Write down: (a) the broad problem in one sentence, (b) the specific, data-answerable research question you formulated and (c) one thing your narrower question necessarily leaves out of scope. Being explicit about (c) is not a weakness in your work — it is exactly the kind of limitation a strong Discussion section names openly.

title: 7  Sustainability Problem Solving
text:
7.3 Data as Evidence, Not Proof
A dataset provides evidence toward answering a sustainability question — it does not provide proof in the way a mathematical theorem does. Two examples worth sitting with:

Finding that mean temperature across five German regions is statistically higher in 2015–2024 than in 1991–2000 (Chapter 3) is evidence consistent with a real warming trend — but it is not, by itself, proof of a cause and 34 years of data from five regions of one country cannot establish a global climate mechanism on their own.
A GHG-emissions dataset showing “higher share of renewable energy correlates with lower emissions” across countries is evidence for the plausibility of the claim — but correlation across countries conflates many differences (industrial structure, wealth, policy history) that a single scatterplot cannot separate out.

This is why Chapters 3 and 4 exist: statistical inference and modelling are the tools that let you say, carefully, how much evidential weight a pattern actually carries.

title: 7  Sustainability Problem Solving
text:
7.4 Considering Alternative Explanations
Before treating a pattern as the explanation, deliberately generate at least one competing explanation and check whether your data can distinguish between them.

Exercise 7.3 — Generate competing explanations
Example: “Does a higher share of renewable energy correlate with lower greenhouse gas emissions?” (the example challenge from an early rubric proposal for this module).
Q1. List at least two explanations for an observed negative correlation between renewable-energy share and emissions, other than “renewables directly cause lower emissions” (for instance: wealthier countries can afford both more renewables and stricter industrial regulation; the causal arrow could run the other way if emissions targets drove renewable investment).
Q2. For your own challenge question, do the same: name one alternative explanation for the pattern you expect (or found) in your data and state whether your current dataset lets you rule it out, partially address it, or not address it at all.

title: 7  Sustainability Problem Solving
section: 7.5 From Evidence to an Evidence-Based Response
text:
7.5 From Evidence to an Evidence-Based Response
The final step connects your analysis back to the sustainability problem you started from and to who might act on it. A useful check: could a specific, named audience (a regional climate-adaptation office, an EU policy team, a citizen-science group) actually do something differently based on your conclusion, stated as you’ve written it?

Exercise 7.4 — Write your evidence-based response
In 3–5 sentences, connect your Exercise 7.1 findings back to the original broad problem: what does your evidence support, what does it leave open and who could act on it and how? This paragraph is close to a first draft of your final report’s Conclusion section (see Chapter 8).

title: 7  Sustainability Problem Solving
section: 7.6 A Short Self-Check: Global Citizenship Competencies
text:
7.6 A Short Self-Check: Global Citizenship Competencies
Goodale, Gilmore and Griffiths (2024) describe six observable competencies that environmental stewardship draws on. You don’t need to master all six to complete this module, but pausing to check where you already stand and where this challenge pushed you, is itself useful material for your final report’s Discussion section.

Rate yourself briefly, a sentence each is enough, on:

Intergroup empathy. Can you describe how this environmental issue is experienced differently in a country or community other than your own?
Valuing diversity. Did your analysis consider more than one region’s, country’s or group’s perspective?
Social justice orientation. Did you consider who is most affected by this problem and whether that differs from who has the most power to address it?
Willingness to sustain the environment. Has working through this challenge changed anything about your own everyday choices, even a small one?
Intergroup helping. Does your Exercise 7.4 response name who could act on it, beyond “someone should do something”?
Responsibility to act. Is there one concrete next step you personally could take or advocate for, based on what you found?




If “narrowing a wicked problem into a data question” feels abstract with no example to anchor it: Our World in Data shows, across hundreds of real topics, how broad global challenges get turned into specific, chart-able questions — browse a few entries close to your own challenge topic before starting Exercise 7.1.


If you want the deeper conceptual framing behind treating sustainability as interconnected systems rather than isolated problems: Kate Raworth’s Doughnut Economics (2017) is the widely-cited starting point and pairs well with this module’s stewardship framing. For the transformative-learning and Global Citizenship Education ideas in this chapter’s opening section, Mezirow (1997) and Rieckmann (2021) are the primary sources; Lotz-Sisitka, Wals, Kronlid and McGarry (2015) go further into transgressive social learning for anyone writing more deeply on this in their final report.

7.7 Check your understanding

Can you narrow a broad sustainability problem into a specific, data-answerable question while keeping the original problem visible in your final conclusion?
Can you name, for your own challenge, at least one alternative explanation for the pattern you found?
Can you state clearly what your evidence does and does not establish?
Can you name one assumption your own frame of reference brought to your dataset, especially if it comes from a context other than your own?

Continue to Chapter 8, Scientific Communication.

title: 8  Scientific Communication
text:
8.1 Know Your Audience
In this area you will learn how to: present findings clearly, select effective visualisations, explain uncertainties and limitations, adapt communication to different audiences and create scientific reports, briefs or dashboards. (Source materials: Data Visualization: A Practical Introduction* (socviz.co), Fundamentals of Data Visualization (clauswilke.com/dataviz) — see Resources.)*
This chapter is where your work from every other competency area comes together into the two required final outputs from the overview: an interactive dashboard and a short scientific report.
The same finding needs different framing for different readers. Before building anything, decide:
Your scientific report is written mainly for the first audience; your dashboard is usually written for something closer to the second, even though both draw on the same underlying analysis.

title: 8  Scientific Communication
text:
A specialist reader (e.g. another data-science student, your instructor) wants methodological detail, model diagnostics and explicit uncertainty.
A policy or general audience wants the headline finding, its practical implications and honest caveats — without needing to parse a regression table.

title: 8  Scientific Communication
text:
8.2 Selecting Effective Visualisations
A good visualisation answers a specific question at a glance; a bad one requires a paragraph of explanation to be understood at all. A few working rules, building directly on the Grammar of Graphics from Chapter 2:

Match the geometry to the question. Comparing categories → bars. Showing change over time → lines. Showing a relationship between two continuous variables → scatterplot. Showing a distribution → histogram or boxplot. Don’t default to a bar chart out of habit when a line or scatterplot answers the question more directly.
Label everything a stranger would need. Axis titles with units, a clear legend, a data source and access date and — for any interval or model estimate — a visible indication of uncertainty (error bars, a shaded confidence band).
Avoid chartjunk. 3D effects, unnecessary gridlines and decorative colour gradients cost attention without adding information. Every visual element should earn its place.
Choose colour deliberately. Use a sequential palette for an ordered quantity, a qualitative palette for unordered categories and check your plot still reads correctly in greyscale or to a colour-blind viewer (scale_colour_viridis_d() in ggplot2 is a reliable default).


Exercise 8.2 — Critique a chart
Take the temperature–sunshine scatterplot you built in Exercise 2.4.
Q1. Would a policy audience understand this plot without your commentary? What is missing — labels, a title that states the finding rather than just the variable names, a caption noting the data source?
Q2. Rebuild it with a title that states a finding (e.g. “More sunshine, slightly higher temperatures, across all five regions”), proper axis labels with units and a caption citing the data source (remember: this is real DWD data, CC BY 4.0 — the caption should say so).

title: 8  Scientific Communication
text:
8.3 Communicating Uncertainty and Limitations Honestly
A dashboard or report that hides its uncertainty is not more convincing — it is less trustworthy once a careful reader notices what’s missing. Concretely:

State confidence intervals, not just point estimates, wherever you computed one in Chapter 3.
Name your model’s assumptions and any you couldn’t fully verify (recall the repeated-measures limitation from Exercise 4.4) — it’s better to name a limitation openly than to present a coefficient as if it came from an ideal, unlimited dataset.
Distinguish explicitly between what your evidence supports and what it does not establish — this is exactly the Exercise 7.4 sentence you already drafted in Chapter 7.

title: 8  Scientific Communication
text:
8.4 Building the Interactive Dashboard
Your final dashboard must be built with shinydashboard, the R package that gives a Shiny app a structured dashboard layout (header, sidebar menu and a grid of boxes) instead of a plain single-page app. This is a deliberate, required choice for this module — not one option among several — because it gives every student’s final output the same recognisable structure and because live, user-driven filtering (picking a region or year range and watching every panel update) is itself part of what this competency area is assessing.


app.R — minimal shinydashboard skeleton

library(shiny)
library(shinydashboard)
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)

climate <- read_csv("data/clean/dwd_climate_clean.csv")

ui <- dashboardPage(
  dashboardHeader(title = "German Regional Climate — DWD, 1991-2024"),
  dashboardSidebar(
    selectInput("period", "Period:", choices = c("1991-2000", "2015-2024", "Both"), selected = "Both"),
    selectInput("region", "Region:", choices = c("All", unique(climate$Region)))
  ),
  dashboardBody(
    fluidRow(
      box(title = "Temperature over time", width = 6, plotlyOutput("temp_plot")),
      box(title = "Precipitation by region",  width = 6, plotlyOutput("precip_plot"))
    ),
    fluidRow(
      box(title = "Key finding", width = 12, textOutput("finding_text"))
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {
  # filter `climate` reactively based on input$period / input$region,
  # then render each plotlyOutput() and the finding_text from that filtered data
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

Required elements — your submitted dashboard must include all of the following, not just a working app shell:

At least two linked, interactive panels (box()es) built with plotly outputs, each addressing a distinct part of your research question — not two views of the same single chart.
At least one input control (selectInput(), sliderInput(), or similar) that actually changes what the panels show — a dashboard where every widget is decorative does not meet this requirement.
Labels a stranger would need: axis titles with units, a legend where relevant and a visible data-source caption (dataset name and access/generation date) somewhere on the page.
A visible indication of uncertainty on at least one panel where you computed one in Chapter 3 (a confidence band, error bars, or the interval stated in a caption) — a dashboard that only shows point estimates hides exactly the information §8.3 asks you to communicate honestly.
One short, written “key finding” panel or caption stating, in plain language, what the dashboard’s main pattern is — the same discipline as a plot title that states a finding rather than just variable names (§8.2).
A short qualitative reflection panel, alongside the key-finding panel: in a sentence or two, who is affected by this pattern, whose data or perspective might be missing from your dataset and why does this local result matter beyond this one place? This is the quantitative-and-qualitative pairing this module asks for and the same habit of mind from Chapter 7 — your dashboard should say something in words, not only in charts.
Deployability. Your app.R (or ui.R/server.R) must run with shiny::runApp() from a clean checkout of your repository — see the Resources page for shinydashboard setup and deployment tutorials (including free hosting via shinyapps.io, if you want a shareable link rather than a local-only app).


Exercise 8.4 — Build your shinydashboard
Using the skeleton above as a starting point, build your dashboard against your own challenge dataset, meeting all seven required elements listed above.
Q3. Show your dashboard to a classmate who hasn’t seen your data. Can they state your main finding back to you, correctly, within 30 seconds of using it? If not, what would you change — a clearer input label, a better chart title, a more prominent key-finding panel?
Q4. Which input control did you choose and why does it matter for your research question specifically (not just “because dashboards usually have filters”)?

title: 8  Scientific Communication
text:
8.5 Writing the Short Scientific Report
Revisit the required structure from the overview’s final-challenge section: Research Question, Environmental Context, Data, Methods, Results, Discussion, Conclusion, References and Data Sources. Write it in the order it will finally appear — this is also the order a reader experiences it in:

Introduction (your Research Question) — state the problem and the specific, data-answerable question you’re addressing.
A short theoretical framing (your Environmental Context) — a few sentences grounding the problem in why it matters and what is already known, not a full literature review.
Methods — document your steps precisely; this doubles as your reproducibility documentation from Chapter 5.
Results — the figures and numbers from Chapters 2–4.
Discussion, drawing directly on your Chapter 7 evidence-based response.
Conclusion.


Ask your learning buddy to read a draft section back to you and ask “what would a reader still want to know here?” rather than asking it to write the section for you outright — the Discussion and Conclusion in particular need to reflect your judgement about what the evidence does and doesn’t support.



If shinydashboard’s ui/server split feels confusing at first: RStudio’s own Shiny tutorial builds up a basic app step by step before introducing the dashboard layout on top of it — work through that first if the skeleton above doesn’t yet make sense.


If you want to go beyond the required elements — better chart design, storytelling structure, or a more polished report: Storytelling with Data (Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic) is the widely-used reference for turning correct charts into genuinely persuasive ones.

Practice Dataset
This page collects the open resources referenced throughout the module, plus the practice dataset used in Rubrics 1–4. Everything here is either open-access or explicitly licensed for reuse — check each source’s own licence before adapting it.
The worked example used across Chapter 1 through Chapter 4 is real, open climate data from the Deutscher Wetterdienst (DWD, Germany’s national meteorological service): annual regional averages of air temperature, precipitation and sunshine duration for five German Bundesländer (Bayern, Sachsen, Nordrhein-Westfalen, Schleswig-Holstein, Baden-Württemberg) plus the national “Deutschland” series, covering 1991–2024 (34 years — long enough to see a real, substantial warming trend). Source: DWD Climate Data Center, regional averages, licensed CC BY 4.0. data/raw/dwd_climate_raw.csv (the real DWD values, with a small number of disclosed, deliberately reintroduced formatting issues for Chapter 1’s data-quality exercises) and data/clean/dwd_climate_clean.csv (tidy, analysis-ready). Full column definitions, exact source URLs and a full disclosure of exactly what was changed for teaching purposes are in data/README.md in the project folder. Regenerate the dataset with data/generate_climate_dataset.py.

About the Blueprint
This module’s structure and tone take inspiration from Christina Bogner’s Environmental Statistics lecture notes (Bookdown, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) — numbered chapters building from data basics through modelling, worked exercises throughout and an appendix of further resources. This module is built in Quarto rather than Bookdown (Quarto is Bookdown/R Markdown’s direct successor, same underlying idea, actively developed), which is why the two sites look different, but the pedagogical shape is deliberately close.
